column1: [Vantage Point] Purging the flood control rot: Will Marcos Jr. sink or swim?
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Raphael Reyes/Rappler President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos in a defiant tone warned that “ no one, not even family members or political allies, will be spared ” from the investigation into corruption  allegations in the scandalous flood control projects. On September 11, 2025, he established the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) through Executive Order 94 . This three-member body will probe irregularities in flood control projects and all national government infrastructure works through the years. The President says being subjected to investigation is a way to determine innocence or guilt. His cousin House Speaker Martin Romualdez, who recently resigned his post, and close ally Representative Zaldy Co of the Ako Bicol partylist are among those implicated in the anomalous flood control projects. The move could be of historical importance. No other sitting Philippine president before Marcos Jr. had called for a probe on massive corruption, vowed to end it, and hold perpetrators accountable. Through the years, the focus of corruption probes has always been the executive, with Congress as the accusing party. But will the President’s bravado match the results? Fairness cannot be expected of either legislative chamber because, as the President pointed out, “Maraming nababanggit na senador … marami ring nababanggit na congressman (Many senators have been named…and many congressmen have also been mentioned).” “ Kaya sinasabi ng mga tao, bakit naman nag-iimbestiga sila (That is why the people are saying, why are they doing the investigation), but they are investigating themselves, which is always a little bit of a difficult situation na (already, and) it’s hard to be fair,” Marcos Jr. said in citing the reason for the formation of an independent probe. The ICI is composed of retired Supreme Court justice Andres Reyes Jr. , who is tasked to carry out the investigation within the bounds of law and the Constitution; former DPWH secretary Rogelio Singson, who is expected to provide the engineering and technical expertise required in assessing the questionable projects; Rossana Fajardo, a certified public accountant who has the inquisitive and critical mind of a forensic accountant that could dissect the financial aspects of the anomalous projects, and Mayor Benjamin Magalong, a former police officer who will put together the evidence needed to secure conviction of those involved. Vantage Point sees the creation of the ICI as more than a political maneuver — it is a crucial corrective measure to address a flawed system where congressional investigations have historically produced more spectacle than substance. The creation of such a body recognizes a central truth: accountability cannot thrive in institutions where self-interest and political posturing overwhelm the pursuit of justice. Congress, for all its constitutional oversight powers, has repeatedly fallen into the trap of using inquiries as platforms for partisan warfare rather than venues for truth-finding. The ongoing hearings on flood control projects illustrate this dysfunction vividly. Instead of a sober dissection of systemic flaws — why billions are poured into projects that either collapse prematurely or fail to mitigate flooding — what the public sees are legislators jousting for soundbites, trading accusations, and conveniently steering scrutiny away from allies. This erodes trust and, more critically, distracts from the evidence trail that could lead to prosecution. By contrast, an independent commission carries both the neutrality and institutional focus that Congress lacks. The commission can cut through political noise and track where the money went, who profited, and why institutional safeguards failed. Its singular mandate will be to map the anatomy of corruption in flood control — without the burden of protecting political patrons or the need to spin narratives for reelection. Critics will argue that Congress has the constitutional duty of oversight, and that relinquishing investigations to a commission undermines this check-and-balance system. This argument, while sound on paper, ignores political reality. The same lawmakers who authorized, lobbied for, or benefitted from flood control projects cannot credibly be the ones to investigate their own complicity. Oversight becomes farcical when the overseer has a vested interest in muddying the trail. What the nation needs is not a duplicative circus of simultaneous inquiries but a disciplined, impartial probe that will command the confidence of the public and withstand judicial scrutiny. For this reason, Congress should step aside — not in abdication of its duty, but in recognition of its conflict of interest. It can play a constructive role later, by legislating reforms based on the ICI’s findings: tightening procurement rules, creating stricter monitoring systems, and enacting safeguards against collusion between contractors and officials. Flood control projects have long been the pork barrel of public works, bleeding billions from the treasury with little to show in terms of real flood mitigation. Marcos’ move to establish an independent commission is thus an opportunity to break this cycle. Congress must resist the temptation to grandstand and instead allow the process to run its course. The Filipino public is tired of inquiries that end in stalemate and scandal fatigue. I’m giving the ICI the benefit of the doubt. It offers a chance — perhaps the last in this cycle of corruption — to pierce the veil of impunity. Congress should allow it to do its work unimpeded. Its role will come later, not as prosecutor, but as reformer: to legislate stricter procurement safeguards, stronger monitoring systems, and airtight penalties for collusion. History offers sobering lessons. The Fertilizer Fund scam hearings conducted by the Senate Committee on Agriculture. Congress hearings in 2006 exposed how billions meant for farmers were siphoned off, yet not a single mastermind was meaningfully punished. The 2007 inquiry into the Philippine National Broadband Network controversy (also referred to as the NBN–ZTE deal or NBN–ZTE mess) became a theater of walkouts and exposés, but no one went to jail despite overwhelming evidence of bribery. The Priority Development Assistance Fund scandal, also called the PDAF scam or the pork barrel scam — perhaps the most infamous — was exposed in 2013 and showcased lawmakers grilling Janet Napoles on prime-time television, even as many of those who had benefitted from her schemes managed to slip away untouched. In all these cases, congressional probes yielded publicity, not justice. If Congress refuses to yield, then history will judge it once more as a body obsessed with theatrics and prone to misrepresentation. If Marcos weakens the ICI, he will be condemned as just another president unwilling to confront entrenched and systemic corruption. But if both Congress and the Palace do what is right, the nation may finally see a corruption probe that delivers results instead of ratings. The independent commission to probe anomalies in flood control projects is both bold and necessary. For decades, congressional investigations have carried the illusion of accountability, but their record betrays a troubling pattern: more smoke than fire, more grandstanding than justice. The ongoing flood control investigation shows the same symptoms. Lawmakers thunder about corruption, but their questions often pivot to protecting allies or undermining rivals. The spectacle dominates headlines while the technical heart of the matter — where the money went, how contracts were rigged, which officials facilitated the graft — remains obscured. Worse, the very lawmakers implicated in the misuse of flood control funds now position themselves as truth-seekers, further eroding the credibility of the entire exercise. But a word of warning must also be addressed to the President: creating a commission is only half the battle. Filipinos have seen too many “independent” bodies neutered into irrelevance. The Agrava Commission on Ninoy Aquino’s assassination , the Melo Commission on political killings, and the Sabio Panel on military corruption all began with high expectations but ended with watered-down reports and no real accountability. Each became a symbol of how commissions can be used to defuse public anger while protecting the powerful. Marcos cannot afford that outcome. He must give the flood control commission teeth — subpoena powers, prosecutorial backing, and full public transparency. Anything less, and it will be dismissed as just another political gimmick. More than that, this commission will test Marcos Jr.’s political capital and his break from the Duterte patronage networks that once nurtured players like the Discayas. If the commission fearlessly investigates not just contractors but the politicians who enabled them — whether allies in Congress or remnants of the Duterte’s camp — it will signal a real shift in how corruption is confronted. If it tiptoes around the powerful, it will expose the President’s reformist stance as hollow. In the end, Marcos faces a defining choice. He can allow the commission to become the hammer that finally smashes the flood control syndicates, or he can let it wither into yet another dusty report in the Palace archives. His legacy hinges on this: will he be remembered as the president who cleaned up flood control, or as another chief executive who promised reform but shielded the guilty and protected the very syndicates he vowed to dismantle? The stakes could not be higher. This is not just about flood control; it is about whether the President can finally redraw the battle lines of accountability in Philippine governance. The move could be of historical importance. No other sitting Philippine president before Marcos Jr. had called for a probe on massive corruption, vowed to end it, and hold perpetrators accountable. The creation of such a body recognizes a central truth: accountability cannot thrive in institutions where self-interest and political posturing overwhelm the pursuit of justice. column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. ‘MANANANGGAL’ PROJECT. Work resumes on a 2022 flood control project in Oriental Mindoro amid the controversy over anomalous flood control projects Bonz Dolor/Facebook MANILA, Philippines — Oriental Mindoro Governor Humerlito “Bonz” Dolor has raised the alarm over billion-peso flood control projects in the province, calling them overpriced, substandard, and, in some cases, “ghost projects.” He made the revelations during a Senate blue ribbon probe on Monday, September 8. Dolor cited a P4-billion flood control project implemented by Sunwest in Sto. Niño, Pinamalayan, which collapsed on October 24, 2024, barely a year after construction. Sunwest, a business conglomerate based in Albay, was co-founded by Ako Bicol Representative Zaldy Co. It is among the top contractors that cornered flood control projects under the Marcos administration. In March 2023, Dolor ordered a 45-day suspension of the project, citing the lack of consultation with the provincial government. During the hearing, Navotas Representative Toby Tiangco linked Co to P3.1 billion worth of budget insertions for Oriental Mindoro. Dolor also criticized the poor construction quality of flood control projects, noting that the metals used were “smaller than my pinky finger.” He added that some structures were hollow and filled only with sand. Based on DPWH’s detailed engineering design, each sheet pile for a flood control project should measure 12 meters. But in Barangay Tagumpay, Naujan, Dolor said the piles driven into the ground are only three meters long. To avoid scrutiny, Dolor said, contractors carried out questionable work at night. He presented a photo taken at 10:40 pm in Barangay Tagumpay, Naujan, as proof. Rappler previously made an explainer about this scheme of flood control contractors. Dolor also pointed out the missing and incomplete projects in his province. A P189-million flood control project in Sitio Dike, Barangay Apitong, Naujan, supposedly handled by Elite General Contractor and Development Corporation — a firm linked to controversial contractors Curlee and Sarah Discaya — was nowhere to be found. Another project worth P50 million in Barangay Buong Lipa, Gloria, contracted to the Discayas’ St. Timothy Construction, was supposed to span 326 meters but only delivered 189 meters in 2023. But when the flood control issue blew up, Dolor said the construction began again, calling it “ mananangal project.” ( Mananangal is a mythical winged creature that separates its upper body from its lower half at night.) The Discayas are linked to at least nine construction firms that were recently disqualified from participating in government biddings. Dolor also alleged corruption behind the projects, claiming he was told by DPWH-Mimaropa Director Gerald Pacanan that contractors needed to set aside 25% “for the higher ups,” a 5% “parking fee,” and another 12% for other cuts. The governor further accused some contractors of engaging in illegal quarrying — “theft of minerals” — and failing to pay quarry taxes. Dolor stressed that the province already had a sound flood mitigation master plan, completed by local and foreign experts and endorsed to the DPWH in 2019 with an estimated cost of P12 billion. From 2022 to 2025, Oriental Mindoro has received P30.29 billion worth of flood control projects, nearly thrice the estimated cost of the province’s flood mitigation plan. Over P17.82 billion of which are from budget insertions. From 2022 to 2025, however, the province received P30.29 billion worth of flood control projects — almost three times the cost of the master plan. Of this, P17.82 billion came from budget insertions. If the master plan had been followed, Dolor said, it would have addressed Oriental Mindoro’s flooding problem. Instead, he lamented, the projects built had designs that looked “more like boulevards,” citing those in San Isidro, Bongabong, and Mulawin, Naujan. — Rappler.com   How does this make you feel?

column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. David Castuciano/Rappler Imagine a ₱10-billion flood control program spread across Bulacan, Pampanga, and Cavite. Under the current, opaque system, this is how Filipino taxpayers’ money is used to fund “ghost projects” and line project proponents’ pockets: Each regional office of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) submits project proposals and progress reports manually. Disbursements would then pass through layers of accounting officers, contractors, and suppliers. These ghost projects — such as dredging that never happened and the construction of weak embankments that would collapse after heavy rainfall — will thereafter be certified “completed.” Auditors face missing receipts, altered logs, and falsified progress reports. Kickbacks are laundered through shell contractors or fake subcontracting chains. Witnesses later allege that as much as 25% of the project cost is siphoned through cash withdrawals and split among lawmakers, district engineers, and private partners. Each monsoon season, when the floodwaters rise across Bulacan, Pampanga, or Cavite, the tragedy is more than meteorological — it’s man-made. Behind every clogged estero, every collapsed embankment, and every vanished floodway lies a paper trail of padded contracts, fake progress reports, and project funds drained long before the first cement truck arrived. Flood control, one of the most capital-intensive programs of the DPWH, has also been one of its most corrupted. Billions of pesos in government funds have been lost to “ghost” dredging, overpriced embankments, and nonexistent canals. What makes this type of corruption especially resilient is its invisibility. Unlike road projects or buildings, flood-control works often lie beneath the surface. Once completed, they’re buried under soil or hidden beneath water — making inspection difficult, if not impossible, for ordinary citizens. Even worse, the paper-based procurement-and-auditing system — reliant on affidavits, signatures, and manual vouchers — offers too many opportunities for collusion. Certificates of completion can be fabricated, receipts misplaced, and project milestones manipulated to justify premature fund releases. column1: ‘Jail the corrupt!’ Flood control corruption sends thousands marching in protest
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. GATHERING STORM. Members of Tindig Pilipinas, Nagkaisa Labor Coalition, Kalipunan ng Kilusang Masa, SIKLAB (Simbahan at Komunidad Laban sa Katiwalian), and Akbayan at the EDSA Shrine prepare to march to the People Power Monument in Quezon City to protest the widespread government corruption on September 11, 2025. Jire Carreon/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – Some wore white to indicate non-partisanship; some, black, to symbolize how government is as rotten as a grave. A woman in Tuguegarao, north of Manila, brought her entire family to the city park, to hopefully teach children not to stand idly by when wrong is being done. A man in Manila carried his dog, switching its name tag with a homemade placard that said, “ Nangangagat ng mga kora p (He bites corrupt people).” Runners and bikers were among the earliest to head to Luneta, the monument to the Philippine national hero, while celebrities showed up, shedding glamour for indignation. Others came on free rides provided by transport groups, while a motorcycle-hailing company offered discounts to passengers going to and coming from the rallies in Luneta and EDSA. At least one man literally wheeled himself — he was a person with disability confined to a wheelchair — across seven kilometers, from Cainta to where protesters were gathered along EDSA. Led mostly by young people, thousands of Filipinos marched in key cities across the Philippines on Sunday, September 21, to protest corruption in government, particularly in flood control projects. Quite poetically, those from up north in Luzon down to some parts of the Visayas marched against flood control project anomalies as rain poured, brought about by Super Typhoon Nando and the southwest monsoon. Student groups, sectoral organizations, religious groups, people of various political persuasions, and unaffiliated concerned citizens condemned those involved in the flood control scandal, while also acknowledging that the syndicate-like dealings had been made possible by a broken system that also needed fixing. More than condemning corruption that had reached dizzying amounts, and beyond calling for sustained vigilance among citizens, protesters cried for justice. Their demand was specific: jail the implicated lawmakers and other elected officials, Department of Public Works and Highways employees, and private contractors — or test the limits of an already outraged public. On social media, weeks before the rallies, a prevailing sentiment was to not just jail the corrupt, but to make them return what they stole from public coffers. There were even scares about protesters staging lightning rallies in posh subdivisions where so-called “policontractors” reside. “I think we did well. We surpassed our expectations,” said Kiko Aquino Dee, a spokesperson for the protest organizers at the People Power Monument, referring to the crowd estimate. Nationwide, an estimated 61,605 people joined protests against government corruption, the Philippine National Police reported. “Everybody was able to express their sentiments, their anger at the grave corruption happening in the Philippines, and we did it in a way that is peaceful. We did it in a way that rejected all of the things outside of the Constitution. We made our voices heard, we renewed our commitment to the spirit of People Power,” Dee told Rappler. The challenge after the rally is sustaining it, he said. “Definitely, the anger is still there. It’s up to us, organizers, to continue to give it venues to express it productively,” he added. While the rallies were organized primarily to protest the trillion-peso anomalies in flood control projects, various groups also took the opportunity to denounce endemic corruption in general, pointing out that both the families of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte were complicit. On Sunday, protesters also commemorated the 53rd anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law by President Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr., father of the incumbent. (READ: Marcos, the dictator’s son, backs September 21 protests vs flood control corruption ) Opposition politicians and celebrities joined the rallies and marches in Luneta in Manila and the People Power Monument in Quezon City, while rallies were also held in Baguio, Tuguegarao, Legazpi, Cebu, Dumaguete, Tacloban, Bacolod, Cagayan de Oro, Butuan, Cotabato, Marawi, and other key cities across the country. Some supporters of Vice President Duterte gathered near the main crowd of protesters on EDSA to call for Marcos’ ouster — which would mean Duterte would take over. (READ: Duterte: I am also corrupt ) The Vice President herself has refused to make public her assets list and to explain the alleged misuse of confidential funds allotted to her office. Her brother Paolo’s district in Davao City got P51 billion in flood control funds in the last half of their father’s presidency. During his State of the Nation Address in July, President Marcos warned against widespread corruption in flood control projects while Filipinos lose lives, livelihood, and belongings to constant floods. He told those involved, “ Mahiya naman kayo! (Be ashamed of yourselves!)” In early August, the President launched a website where citizens could check flood control projects and submit information on anomalous projects in their localities. A week before that, Rappler had already launched the FloodControlPH channel on the Rappler app to crowdsource leads for possible investigative pieces. Marcos identified 15 contractors which had cornered 1 in every 5 flood control projects across the country in the last 3 years, or under his administration. Five of them turned out to have bagged multi-billion-peso contracts despite not having enough capital . Later, he created the Independent Commission for Infrastructure that would investigate all possible public works and infrastructure corruption in the last 10 years. This means the probe covers the six years Rodrigo Duterte was president, when lawmakers, DPWH engineers, and private contractors were supposed to have perfected flood control fund misuse, which is deemed less detectable than those involving other infrastructure allocations. The Senate and the House of Representatives are conducting their own probes into the anomalous projects, although citizens have expressed doubts about where these would lead, as lawmakers are among those alleged to have benefited from corruption. A few DPWH engineers have either been dismissed from service or placed on preventive suspension , while several more are on the immigration lookout list . The Anti-Money Laundering Council has frozen hundreds of bank accounts linked to the persons being investigated. While some quarters are hoping that Sunday’s protest would snowball into something akin to the People Power Revolution of 1986 , others were concerned until when the rage would hold. What is clear to Obet Sumayao, the wheelchair-bound protester from Cainta, Rizal, is this: At least before he dies, he wants to see the crooks behind bars. – with reports from Aries Rufo Journalism Fellows 2025 , Roland Andam Jr., Iya Gozum, Gemma Mendoza, Paterno Esmaquel II/Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

column1: [OPINION] Flood control latest sign of government ‘greenwashing’
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Today marks the 16th anniversary of Tropical Storm Ondoy , which, in many ways, first opened the eyes of the Filipino nation to the reality of the climate crisis. Still, it took until earlier this year for the reported climate budget to exceed P1 trillion, or more than double of the previous year’s allocation. This seemed like a good sign that the entire government was finally ramping up its climate actions. However, from what we know now, it turns out it was too good to be true. Congressional sessions and agency meetings over the years have mostly emphasized the leading roles of agencies such as the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in climate action. The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is not mentioned nearly as often, yet it is the agency with by far the largest share of the domestic climate budget. It has 89% of the allotment under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA) . Over P350 billion from its P1-trillion allocation was given to flood control projects, a slight increase from 2024. Today, the DPWH finds itself at the epicenter of the worst corruption scandal in recent years because of the anomalies related to flood control. Many across the nation took to the streets last Sunday, September 21, demanding an end to the culture of impunity that has manifested many times before. In reference to a previous Rappler op-ed , these peaceful protests may be the “tipping point” for a renewed nationwide demand for genuine good governance. Because there may be more in this climate budget that needs to be looked into. In the 2025 GAA, the DPWH budget also featured more than P330 billion for the construction of new roads, ports, and other infrastructure to “climate-resilient design standards.” An additional P216.8 billion was allotted for retrofitting assets and capital “to protect against climate change and climate variability”; examining the document showed these assets and capital largely also pertain to roads. The reputation of road construction and repairs in the Philippines is perhaps even more notorious than flood control projects. Given the similarities in issues often observed among these projects, conducting an extensive national investigation on road repair and construction projects should also be done under the current administration. This context has influenced the Department of Agriculture to begin an audit of all farm-to-market roads since 2021. For all projects in the 2025 GAA contributing to food security, more than 60% of the allotted budget went to actions connected to “production and distribution systems,” which is largely dedicated to farm-to-market road projects. Assuming the allegations regarding corruption in flood control projects are true, these point to acts of greenwashing by some government agencies and officials. Misleading the public through claims of decisions supposedly being environment-friendly to mask corrupt practices does not just apply to the private sector. For the current administration, which has made climate action a priority agenda, this would cause even more damage to its reputation domestically and even at the global level. South Korea certainly has taken notice of the implications of these scandals. The way to trace which projects are aligned with national climate objectives is through the Climate Change Expenditure Tagging (CCET). Under this system, projects can be classified as contributing to adaptation or mitigation, and to the seven thematic areas under the country’s National Climate Change Action Plan (e.g., food security, water sufficiency, human security). It is intended to provide a transparent means of monitoring public funds spent on climate projects and inform decision-making. Instead, aside from the obvious imperative to purge corruption, the flood control scandals have exposed the weaknesses of the CCET system that need to be addressed if we want to avoid these incidents. Firstly, it is absurd to have so much of the national climate budget concentrated on only one agency. The executive and legislative branches must ensure a more even spread of public funds to address climate-relevant issues, including food security, water sufficiency, and sustainable energy through renewable energy. Secondly, there must be more support for strengthening monitoring and evaluation by the mandated agencies, the CCC and the Department of Budget and Management. Some of the billions of pesos from flood control projects can be reallotted to capacity-building for them to fulfill these tasks. Thirdly, there needs to be a stronger quality assurance for ensuring projects contribute to climate action. The current practice of agencies doing their own tagging needs to be reexamined and revised to ensure their proposed actions are justified as climate-tagged, not just for compliance or the appearance of one. column1: Pulangi River erosion threatens BARMM highway amid PH flood control scandals
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. DANGER. The Pulangi River slowly eats away at the riverbank in Pagalungan, Maguindanao del Sur, eroding soil beneath a national highway and threatening its collapse. DPWH XII COTABATO CITY, Philippines – A vital stretch of highway in Maguindanao del Sur is on the brink of crumbling into the Pulangi River, a collapse that could sever one of key arteries in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The river, swollen and unruly after shifting its course, has chewed dangerously close to the Cotabato-Davao Highway. In Barangay Layog, Pagalungan town, just a sliver of earth now stands between the road and the encroaching current. Authorities have reduced traffic to a single lane, but this has created crippling congestion on a route that carries the lifeblood of trade and travel across the region. Local officials have sounded alarm bells, but their pleas come at a time when public trust in flood control programs is badly shaken. Across the country, scandals over padded contracts and ghost projects have hollowed out public confidence, casting doubt on whether urgent fixes in Maguindanao del Sur will arrive before the river takes the highway section itself. For some of them, the scandals explain why towns like Pagalungan – where a section of a national highway is several heavy rainfalls away from being swept into the Pulangi River – have been starved of funds for decades. “This situation is very alarming, and is in need of immediate action,” Maguindanao del Sur Representative Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu said during an on-site inspection on Saturday, August 23, with former Pagalungan mayor and now Councilor Salik Mamasabulod. The Pulangi River, flowing from the mountains of Bukidnon and Cotabato, altered its course in recent years, displacing families and submerging farmlands. Its floodwaters are now gnawing at the national highway embankment, threatening to cut off a critical link between Cotabato and Davao. Mamasabulod noted that Pagalungan last received flood control funding in 1982, or 43 years ago, and estimated that at least 500 meters of embankment must be reinforced to protect the road and a nearby bridge. He said at least P200 million is needed immediately to stabilize the riverbank. BARMM Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua, who also inspected the site, has ordered the region’s ministers to respond swiftly. But under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, national highways remain under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), while the BARMM Ministry of Public Works handles provincial and local projects. The erosion has left residents anxious as heavy rain threatens to accelerate the damage. For families who have lost their homes and farms, and for traders who rely on the Cotabato-Davao corridor, the threat is immediate. Local officials called on Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan to use emergency funds for repairs and prevent the likely collapse of an approximately 500-meter section of the highway. Mangudadatu said. “If that happens, the highway will be spared from destruction and our commuters traveling between Davao City and Cotabato, vice versa, will no longer face delays.” He warned that the loss of the road section would have wide-ranging economic consequences, disrupting commerce and raising transport costs across central and southern Mindanao. Both the Bangsamoro region’s transportation and trade ministries have echoed concerns about the dangers ahead. At an August 20 hearing of the House committee on public works and highways, Mangudadatu  pressed DPWH officials on what he described as unequal allocation of funds. “Why are the needs of the people there not the same as the needs of the people in other places?” he asked, pointing out that while Region XII received P196 billion in allocations, the BARMM received only a P92-billion block grant. For now, the community is relying on stopgap measures, with some firms volunteering equipment and resources to install sheet piles on the eroded bank to prevent further collapse. “We just have to rely on ourselves for now,” Mangudadatu said. During his last State of the Nation Address (SONA), President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. publicly rebuked those behind alleged corruption in the country’s flood control projects, short of calling them betrayals of public trust that leave communities defenseless against disasters. Marcos’ remarks triggered a string of exposés that tied overpriced and substandard projects to some lawmakers, Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials, and favored contractors. The revelations have set off investigations that uncovered padded budgets, questionable contracts, and projects that existed only on paper. Billions of pesos meant for levees, drainage systems, and riverbank protections were siphoned off, leaving flood-prone provinces with little more than collapsed dikes and unpaved embankments. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. DESTROYED. Batangas Congressman Leandro Leviste's team inspects flood control projects in the province's first legislative district in August 2025. Lingkod Legarda Leviste/Facebook MANILA, Philippines –The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) removed its proposed P252-billion budget for all locally funded flood control projects from the 2026 national expenditure program, following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive . This brings the agency’s proposed budget down to P625.8 billion from the initial P881 billion. The P15.77-billion budget for foreign-assisted flood control projects next year was retained. “The Department has exerted its best efforts, within the very limited period allotted, to ensure that the issues raised in the previously submitted budget, such as the funding of completed and duplicate projects, are adequately addressed,” DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said in his letter addressed to House Speaker Martin Romualdez and appropriations committee chairperson Mika Suansing. The agency’s flood control projects have been under scrutiny in recent weeks after the government uncovered substandard and ghost projects across the country. Some government officials — including senators , congressmen , and DPWH personnel — are alleged to have benefited from these projects. The DPWH also trimmed P3 billion worth of duplicate or completed projects, including overlapping road sections, rock netting, and cat’s eye and stud installations. In total, the agency’s proposed budget was slashed by P255 billion, or nearly 29%. column1: ‘Widespread destruction, tampering’ of flood project documents at DPWH – ICI
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. MANILA, Philippines – The Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) said on Monday, September 22, that it has received reports of “widespread destruction and tampering of official documents” by some Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials in connection with anomalous flood control projects. “Such acts constitute not only a blatant obstruction of ongoing investigations but also a direct assault on the public’s right to transparency and accountability,” ICI chairperson Andres Reyes Jr. said in a statement, as the fact-finding body expressed its strong condemnation of the reported acts. “The deliberate concealment or alteration of records undermines the rule of law and weakens the people’s trust in government institutions tasked to safeguard public resources,” Reyes added. DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said in an interview that the “suspected tampering and destruction of documents” occurred at the Baguio City District Engineering Office, based on a report from Baguio City Mayor Benjamin Magalong, who also serves as special adviser to the ICI. Dizon said he had already filed a formal complaint against Baguio City District Engineer Rene Zarate and ordered his preventive suspension. He linked the destruction of records to Magalong’s earlier report that the Baguio engineering office had been uncooperative with the ICI. The secretary added that he had tasked retired police general Arthur “Ato” Bisnar to investigate the incident. Bisnar, whom Dizon recommended for the post of DPWH undersecretary, has yet to receive his appointment papers. The agency is undergoing a purge following Dizon’s directive for the courtesy resignation of top officials, including undersecretary Cathy Cabral. “ This serves as a warning to everyone in DPWH. Huwag na huwag kayong magta-tamper or magsisira ng ebidensya, kasi mahuhuli at mahuhuli din kayo, ” Dizon said. (Do not tamper with or destroy evidence, because you will eventually be caught.) Dizon also issued a memo directing officials to preserve and submit to the ICI all documents related to infrastructure projects over the past 10 years. Those who fail to comply, he warned, will face both criminal and administrative complaints. This follows an earlier DPWH memo instructing full cooperation with the ICI investigation. The ICI stressed that all records relating to public works are public property. Reyes urged DPWH officials to cooperate with the probe and preserve the integrity of all documents and evidence in their custody. The commission said that it remains “steadfast in its mandate to uncover the truth behind anomalous flood control projects and to ensure that those responsible are held accountable.” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. created the ICI to investigate flood control and other infrastructure projects in the past 10 years. Some DPWH officials in Bulacan have been placed under preventive suspension , while top officials from the Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office — including Henry Alcanatara , Brice Hernandez , Jaypee Mendoza , and Juanito Mendoza — have been dismissed. Senate President Tito Sotto III and Senate blue ribbon committee chairman Panfilo “Ping” Lacson met with the ICI on Monday to shed light on budget procedures, including how individual and institutional amendments and insertions in the national budget are carried out. “We want to go as far as reaching the original sin. And the original sin is Congress,” Lacson said. “ Kung walang nag-insert, walang paglalaruan ‘yung mga district engineering offices e. We’re mulling on the idea na magusap ‘yung House at Senate, mag-self-restraint na kami. ‘Wag na kaming mag-insert especially sa mga local infrastructure projects na nasa level ng DEO .” (If there are no insertions, the district engineering offices won’t have anything to play with. We’re considering the idea of the House and Senate talking it out and exercising self-restraint. We should stop making insertions, especially in local infrastructure projects handled at the DEO level.) Lacson added that the blue ribbon committee has also retrieved additional evidence from Brice Hernandez, who earlier accused senators Joel Villanueva and Jinggoy Estrada of receiving kickbacks. The senators had categorically denied the allegation. Hernandez, who is under Senate custody after being cited in contempt, was temporarily allowed to leave on Saturday, September 20, to retrieve evidence to back up his claims. Lacson said the panel has yet to open the files gathered by Hernandez due to a technical problem. “ Hindi pa namin na-unseal kasi nagkaroon ng kaunting glitch kasi naiwan ‘yung computer but sealed naman ‘yun ,” Lacson said. (We haven’t unsealed it yet because there was a slight glitch because the computer was left behind, but it’s sealed),” Lacson said. Lacson said that he is discussing the retrieval of the computer with lawyers and Hernandez. “We want to preserve the integrity of the evidence by preserving the chain of custody,” Lacson said. In the House of Representatives, Speaker Bojie Dy said the wanted to suspend the House probe into anomalous flood control projects and turn over the investigation to ICI. He acknowledged public skepticism over the chamber’s inquiry, noting that some lawmakers are either tied to contractors or are contractors themselves. – Rappler.com   How does this make you feel?

column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. FLOOED MANILA. Pedestrians wade through knee-deep floodwaters along Taft Avenue in Manila after heavy rains caused by a low pressure area, on August 22, 2025. Angie de Silva/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – Nearly all or 97% of Filipinos believe that corruption in government is “widespread,” according to the results of Pulse Asia Research, Incorporated survey conducted in late September and released on Wednesday, October 15. The survey also noted the prevailing opinion among Filipinos (90%) that government officials colluded in anomalous projects. Based on the survey findings, a “huge majority” or 85% of adult Filipinos believe that corruption in government increased over the past year, compared to 3% who thought otherwise and 12% who observed no difference. The Pulse Asia survey was conducted from September 27 to 30, among 1,200 representative adults. It has a ± 2.8% error margin at the 95% confidence level; subnational estimates for the geographic areas in the survey have the following error margins at 95% confidence level: ± 5.7% for Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. During and before the survey period, headlines were dominated by congressional probes into anomalous flood control projects that were triggered by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s crackdown on corruption in infrastructure projects , and his creation of the Independent Commission for Infrastructure tasked to investigate anomalies in flood control and other infrastructure projects in the last 10 years. The survey showed that a majority or 54% of Filipinos believe “that the congressional investigations into flood control projects are being conducted to expose corruption in government and to hold accountable those found responsible for irregularities in these projects” while the same percentage are of the view that congressional investigations “are being held for the purpose of exposing corruption in government.” Fewer Filipinos or 19% believe the congressional investigations are “in response to the public’s outrage against corruption in government”; 13% believe they are tools of lawmakers “either to pressure their political rivals or to protect their allies”; while 13% view them “as a diversionary tactic to draw public attention away from other issues.” Pulse Asia also said that the “plurality view” among Filipinos is that the investigations of both houses of Congress are likely to bring out the truth and “to hold those involved accountable.” “The investigations into flood control projects held by the Senate and the House of Representatives are likely to find out the truth on the matter, according to sizable to big pluralities of adults in the country (45% and 38%, respectively),” the pollster said. Editor’s Note: An earlier version of this story reported that fewer Filipinos believe that legislative probes have an impact in exposing corruption. This has been corrected. Fewer Filipinos believe that legislative probes have no impact in exposing corruption: Pulse Asia said “public opinion regarding the trustworthiness of public and private entities involved in addressing the problem of corruption in flood control projects is mixed,” but among these entities, media and civil society organizations are the most trusted in terms of their ability to help in the fight against corruption in flood control projects. “At least half of Filipino adults trust in the ability of civil society organizations (50%) and the media (51%) to help in addressing the problem of corruption in flood control projects in the country. However, a different picture emerges when one considers government entities,” Pulse Asia said. Pulse Asia said a big majority of Filipinos (81%) distrusts the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), while “distrust is the plurality sentiment toward the President (45%).” Ironically, it was Marcos who initiated the investigation into corruption in government, following this State of the Nation Address in late July highlighted by his avowed fight against corrupt DPWH officials and their accomplices in the private sector, followed by the creation of the ICI. The Pulse Asia survey also showed that Filipinos are ambivalent toward the months-old ICI, as 56% of adults cannot say if they trust or distrust the body. “Basically the same percentages either trust the Senate (37%) or are undecided toward its trustworthiness (36%). Likewise, the Office of the Ombudsman registers virtually the same trust and indecision figures (39% versus 43%). As for the House of Representatives, nearly the same percentages either distrust the legislative chamber (36%) or cannot say if they trust or distrust it (40%),” Pulse Asia said. Despite the general distrust for government in the fight against corruption, a big majority or 71% of Filipinos believe “government officials found responsible for the anomalous flood control projects will be punished.” Meanwhile, a survey conducted by Octa Research also during the period — from September 25 to 30 — showed similar findings: a majority of Filipinos are outraged by the corruption in government infrastructure projects. “Most adult Filipinos (60%) reported feeling anger or outrage when they think about corruption in government, particularly in projects such as flood control initiatives. This strong emotional response highlights the public’s continued frustration over the misuse of public funds in infrastructure programs and may suggest declining confidence in the integrity of public institutions,” Octa said. The survey was conducted from September 25 to 30, 2025, among 1,200 respondents through face-to-face interviews. It has a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of ±3%. Across major geographical areas, anger or outrage is highest in Balance Luzon (64%), followed by Visayas (63%), then the National Capital Region (59%), and Mindanao (46%). Notably, anger is also the dominant emotion among the ABC class (70%) and the highest among the socio-economic classes. “Across age groups, the majority of adult Filipinos expressed anger or outrage over corruption in government projects — an emotion especially pronounced among younger Filipinos, particularly Gen Z and millennials,” Octa noted. Meanwhile, the anger emotion is slightly lower at 44% among those aged 65 to 74 . Similarly, a Pulse Asia survey conducted in September showed that corruption (51%) is the second most important issue for Filipinos, following inflation, which topped the list at 54%. Concern about corruption rose significantly from 24% in the June survey, while concern over inflation dropped from 62% during the same period. Notably, the Marcos administration’s approval rating for its efforts to fight corruption dropped to 17% in September, down from 28% in June. Forty-six percent of Filipinos believe that the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) is the “most suitable” body to investigate the flood control scandal. “This finding reflects a strong public preference for a credible, impartial, and non-political inquiry into corruption allegations. Support for the ICI is consistent across all major areas and socioeconomic classes, with particularly high trust levels in the National Capital Region (60%) and among Class ABC (63%),” Octa said. The Senate blue ribbon committee is second with only 23% of Filipinos believing that it is the “appropriate institution” to lead the probe. The Senate panel held its last public inquiry on September 25, when several senators were named as recipients of alleged kickbacks from the infrastructure projects. The Senate committee has yet to schedule its next hearing, pending the appointment of a new chairman. Senator Erwin Tulfo, the panel’s vice chair, has been designated as acting chair. However, critics argue that the Senate lacks the integrity to lead the investigation, as some of its members have been implicated in the controversy. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

column1: PANOORIN: Bilyon-bilyon ang pondo para sa flood control projects. Bakit baha pa rin?
column4: MANILA, Philippines – Matagal nang problema ang baha sa Pilipinas. May mga proyekto ang gobyerno para maibsan ito. Magkano nga ba ang napupunta sa Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) para sa kanilang flood management programs? Panoorin ang report na ito ni Patrick Cruz. Delubyo na ang pondong ibinuhos ng gobyerno sa flood control projects. Ang napala natin? Delubyo rin. Bilyon-bilyon kada taon ang budget para sa flood control. Ngayong 2025, higit P248 billion ang nakuhang budget ng DPWH para sa flood control. Mula 2023 to 2025 sa ilalim ni President Ferdinand Marcos Jr .: P675 billion na ang total. Sa panahon ni president Rodrigo Duterte (2017–2022): P612.28 billion. Kay dating pangulong Noynoy Aquino (2011–2016): P181.7 billion. Sa loob ng nakalipas na 15 taon, umabot na sa P1.47 trillion ang nailaan ng gobyerno para lang sa flood management ng DPWH. Lahat ‘yan, pera ng bayan. Pera mo. Pera natin. Malalim at matagal nang problema ang baha sa Pilipinas. Kapag may baha, paralisado ang transportasyon , suspendido ang klase , apektado ang kabuhayan ng marami, maraming bahay ang lubog, at sa mga nakalipas na mga taon, daan-daan na ang namatay. Maraming dahilan ang pagbaha. ‘Andyan ang problema sa basura, poor urban planning, at climate change. Flood control sana ang isa sa mga solusyon. Bilyon-bilyon na ang nagastos sa flood control projects, pero tuwing umuulan, lubog pa rin ang Pilipinas. Ulan ba talaga ang problema o ang sistema? Ano sa tingin mo? Isabela 6th District Representative Faustino 'Bojie' Dy III gives a speech after replacing House Speaker Martin Romualdez, at the House of Representatives on September 17, 2025. Jire Carreon/Rappler MANILA, Philippines – New Speaker Bojie Dy said he wants the House to suspend its investigation into anomalous flood control projects and let the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) take the lead. “If it were only up to me, regarding infra comm, all reports and whatever happened in the infra comm should already be submitted to the ICI. After all, many of our fellow citizens don’t really believe what’s happening in the infra comm. I think it would be better if we just forward it to the ICI,” Dy told reporters on Monday, September 22, in his first ambush interview with the press. The House kicked off its probe into flood control corruption in August, weeks before Malacañang created the ICI. So far, the House has invited to the hearing top flood control contractors such as Curlee Discaya, and Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials allegedly involved in the modus operandi, such as Henry Alcantara and Brice Hernandez. The inquiry has so far unearthed alleged links of senators Joel Villanueva and Jinggoy Estrada to the DPWH kickback scheme. There remains, however, skepticism from the public about the House investigation, since dozens of lawmakers have alleged ties to contractors or are contractors themselves. The committee, for example, only recently sent an invitation to Ako Bicol Representative Zaldy Co, founder of scandal-ridden contractor Sunwest and co-architect of the highly controversial 2025 national budget. There have also been allegations that congressmen connive with their district engineers to insert pet projects into their funding requests even before the executive’s proposed national budget is turned over to Congress. – Rappler.com  How does this make you feel?

column1: [OPINION] Flood control issue brings PH to ‘tipping point’
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. Why only now? After all, in July, a tropical cyclone whose local name starts with ‘C’ hit the Philippines and, with the southwest monsoon, brought massive flooding across the nation. This caused casualties and billions of pesos’ worth of damages to agriculture, livelihoods, and properties. It then led to widespread criticisms of flood control projects, which has a large share of the national budget, and calls for investigations. What was just mentioned is what actually happened last year, with “Carina.” And this happened again this year, with “Crising.” So why only now? Obviously, there have been public criticisms over failures like this before 2024 and 2025, but why is it only now that the outcry reached this level where it can no longer be ignored or overlooked? There are many factors that contributed to this. We can point to the President making accountability on mismanaged flood control projects a clear priority, as seen in his most recent State of the Nation Address (SONA). While a welcomed move only if there is a clear follow through, this is also political damage control regarding the administration’s public image that may not necessarily be reflected in public surveys. He did present the completion of over 5,500 flood control projects in last year’s SONA, which makes the current scandals even more harmful to how the public sees him and his administration. His candidates also had a relatively-underwhelming performance in the mid-term elections. We can also point to the public now having faces with whom to associate this form of corruption and incompetence. Among the ones drawing the most flak are influencers that also happen to be children of politicians and businesses, many of whom are directly linked to flood control projects. These so-called “nepo-babies” flaunting their luxury clothes, designer bags, and first-class trips on social media is not exactly a new development; they have been doing this for years. But contrasting their lavish lifestyles with the poverty, disasters, and other issues most of the nation are left to endure time and again has become an effective short-term way to make this issue relatable to ordinary Filipinos. We could look into these factors, among others, for reaching this point. Or it could be as simple as Filipinos simply having enough of wading through deep floods, cleaning their houses and streets, and losing income every single year — these days, it could now be every few months. Unfortunately, that last point can be interpreted as Filipinos once again only reacting to a problem when it directly affects them, no matter how long-running the issues are, when it has become more than just an occasional inconvenience. But better late than never, I guess. Some folks would call it a breaking point. But we will use “tipping point.” In scientific discourse, this is known as the moment when a series of small incidents over time cause a drastic and irreversible change in a system. In the context of the climate crisis, this would refer to continued global warming caused by pollution from human activities that cause widespread shifts in the likes of the water cycle and sea surface temperatures; both of these contribute to occurrences of extreme rainfall, formation of typhoons, and rising sea levels. But these days, it has never been clearer that this point would happen even faster through sheer impunity. And it has even more far-reaching effects than most people would realize. While flood control gets by far the most attention in the national climate discourse, as obviously important as this issue is, it is only one part of the national climate strategy. Unknown to most of the nation, many of the Philippines’ climate plans are being updated or developed in 2025. Many of these plans come with a condition — developed countries must provide finance and other means of support, largely because they are responsible for causing the climate crisis and aligned with the nation’s calls for climate justice to the global community. However, developed nations have failed to deliver not just to the Philippines, but other developing countries. For example, in the country’s current plan for reducing climate pollution, less than one percent of the estimated P4 trillion needed for its full implementation has been received about halfway through this decade. To make it worse, most of the support we end up getting from developed countries is in the form of loans. Translation: the public will end up paying this back, in one way or another. These billions of pesos wasted on these failed flood control projects could have been used to reduce the dependence on these loans and, subsequently, the country’s rising debt under the current government. They could have been used to prevent even more economic and non-economic losses and damages. That money could have been used for protecting our forests, helping our farmers, or actually mitigating floods. As much as the Philippine government rightfully echoes the call for accountability by global polluters, we must demand for accountability in our backyard. And this is where another way to look at the concept of ‘tipping point’ comes in. In the context of climate action, this would refer to people having a dramatic and more permanent shift in their behaviors and norms. In the current context, this would entail no longer simply treating disasters as an annual inconvenience, accountability as secondary to political patronage, and good governance as measured by popularity and immediate relief. We have the right to be skeptical. We have seen the reactions, the memes, and the outrage on social media before for a few months, before slowly going silent. We have seen previous pursuits of justice turned instead into a game of political machinations. But this time has to be different. The question is which of these tipping points the Philippines would reach first: the climate crisis, or climate action itself. The correct answer is the latter — and it must happen sooner than later. – Rappler.com A climate analyst, John Leo is the National Coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, the Philippines’ leading civil society network on climate action. He is also the Deputy Executive Director for Programs and Campaigns of Living Laudato Si’ Philippines. How does this make you feel?

column1: Marcos eyes ‘economic sabotage’ cases vs contractors of big ghost flood control projects
column4: SUMMARY This is AI generated summarization, which may have errors. For context, always refer to the full article. PROOF. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. shows media receipts as proof that the government has fully paid for the non-existent reinforced concrete riverwall project in Baliuag, Bulacan, on August 20, 2025. Presidential Communications Office MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday, August 20, that his government is eyeing “economic sabotage” cases against contractors of big ghost flood control projects. Marcos made the statement in response to questions at a media interview in Purok 4, Barangay Piel in Baliuag, Bulacan, where he verified a citizen’s complaint about a non-existent — but fully paid for — P55-million reinforced concrete riverwall project Asked about the special fraud audit of the Commission on Audit on flood control projects in Bulacan, Marcos said the ghost project in Baliuag is an “example of falsification… because it was reported as completed.” “Kitang-kita naman na hindi completed. So, immediately that’s a falsification. So, that’s already a very big violation. And for the big ones, talagang I’m thinking very hard to — pipilahan natin sila ng economic sabotage,” he said. “ Tingnan natin, ha, ‘yung utang ng gobyerno ng Pilipinas, ng Republika, ay mababawasan kung naging maayos lahat itong pag-ano. Kasi ngayon babalikan na natin ngayon ito, saan napunta ‘yung pera? Hahabulin natin, kakasuhan natin sila. How long will that take? Hindi ba? ” he added. (It’s evident that it’s not complete. So immediately, that’s falsification. So, that’s already a very big violation. And for the big ones, I’m really thinking very hard to line up economic sabotage [cases against them]. Just look, the Philippine government’s debts would be reduced if these projects were done well. Because now, we have to go back to them — where did the money go to? We will run after them, file cases against them. How long will it take? Right?) In a Facebook post later that day, Marcos announced that he had ordered the blacklisting of SYMS Construction Trading, and also said that it will be charged for violation of Republic Act 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents. “Ang SYMS Construction Trading ay agad na iba-blacklist at haharap sa mga kaso sa ilalim ng Revised Penal Code at RA 3019. Hahanapin at sisiyasatin pa natin ang iba pa nilang proyekto. Hindi natin palalampasin ito. Sususpendihin at kakasuhan ang lahat ng opisyal na nag-authorize at nakipagsabwatan dito,” Marcos said. (SYMS Construction Trading has been immediately blacklisted and will face charges under the Revised Penal Code and RA 3019. We will scrutinize their other projects. We will not let this pass. We will suspend and file cases against officials who authorized [the projects] and connived with them.) Marcos told the media in Baliuag that he went to Barangay Piel, acting on a report his office received through his “citizens’ complaint Sumbong sa Pangulo” website. Upon inspection, he saw no progress or activity for the 220-meter project that cost the government  P55,730,911.60. As of June, Marcos said, the report stated that it was “100% complete and also fully paid.” The Presidential Communications Office posted the official receipts of the payment of the Department of Public Works and Highways Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office to Malolos-based SYMS Construction Trading: the first payment of P43,492,098 on March 19, 2025, and P5,948,792.98 on June 30, 2025. “Wala kaming makita na kahit isang… hollow block, isang ano ng semento, walang equipment dito. Lahat itong project na ito ghost project. Walang ginawa na trabaho dito,” he told the media. (We didn’t see even a single… hollow block, any cement, no equipment here. This is a ghost project. No work was done here.) “I’m not disappointed. I’m angry,” he also said. Marcos said there was an ongoing flood control project on the other side of the riverbank, and that the two contractors involved were “pointing fingers” at each other, explaining that the riverwall project could not begin until the other project was finished. Adding to the mystery, he said, was the difficulty in locating the contract for the project. Marcos suspects that the record was “lost” as the project was repeatedly subcontracted, and the chief district engineer had been replaced over the years. The ones in charge are looking for the records, he said. “Since we put up the website, ang dami talagang sumusulat (many people have messaged us) and this a perfect example of the abuse that is being done by some of these contractors,” Marcos said. “Ongoing naman ‘yung ating mga investigation. Pinag-aaralan namin lahat. Tinitingnan namin lahat ng mga sinusumbong sa amin. And we will not stop. We will keep going until ma-identify na mabuti at makasuhan nang mabuti lahat itong mga contractor at kung sinoman ang mga nakakuha ng kontrata,” he added. (All of the investigations are ongoing. We are studying all of this. We are checking all of the complaints we receive. And we will not stop. We will keep going until all these contractors and anyone else who got contracts are identified and sued.) Marcos said the modus of some contractors is to secure the government contract, and then “sell” the contract to a subcontractor. “Bahala na kung ‘yung subcontractor kung itutuloy niya ‘yung project. Bahala na sila kung maganda, kung sub – kung nasa standard o substandard kaya napapabayaan. At ‘yung iba, hindi na lang itinutuloy.… Anyway, we will keep going. Hahabulin natin silang lahat,” the President said. (The subcontractor will decide if they will continue the project. It would be up to them if [the project] is standard or substandard, that’s why it gets neglected. And there are those who just don’t continue [the project]. Anyway, we will keep going. We will run after all of them.) Marcos earlier bared a list of the top 15 contractors of flood control projects in the country, based on the initial findings of an audit he had ordered during his recent State of the Nation Address (SONA). Of these firms, six received ratings of “unsatisfactory” or “poor” in previous years . The Senate blue ribbon committee has begun probing anomalous flood control projects. – Rappler.com How does this make you feel?

SOUL, CONSCIENCE AND GUILT

Soul, conscience, and guilt are interconnected concepts
where the soul is considered the essence of a person, the conscience is the internal moral compass that guides the soul, and guilt is the emotional pain or negative feeling that arises when one acts against their conscience. Acting in accordance with one's conscience leads to a "clear conscience," while violating it results in a "guilty conscience," which can be a powerful motivator for seeking change or forgiveness. 
Soul
• The soul is considered the essential part of a person, sometimes viewed as the source of one's moral and spiritual being.

Conscience
• The conscience is the internal faculty that allows a person to distinguish right from wrong.
• It functions as a moral guide or "compass" for the soul.
A healthy conscience can be a source of freedom, while a "seared" or ignored conscience can be dangerous, according to some interpretations. 
Guilt
• Guilt is the emotional and psychological response to having violated one's own conscience or sense of right and wrong.
• It is often described as a painful feeling or "bad feeling" that comes from knowing or thinking you have done something wrong.
• The intensity of guilt can depend on the perceived severity of the wrong action, both in relation to others and to oneself.
• Overcoming guilt often involves a process of seeking forgiveness, repenting, and trying to live according to one's conscience in the future. 

The statement "You have no conscience" describes a profound lack of morality and empathy. 
A conscience is the internal sense of right and wrong, and its absence means someone has no regard for the rights or feelings of others. Individuals without a conscience may be very antisocial, can be manipulative, and may not feel guilt or remorse for the harm they cause.

SOUL, CONSCIENCE AND GUILT

Soul, conscience, and guilt are interconnected concepts
where the soul is considered the essence of a person, the conscience is the internal moral compass that guides the soul, and guilt is the emotional pain or negative feeling that arises when one acts against their conscience. Acting in accordance with one's conscience leads to a "clear conscience," while violating it results in a "guilty conscience," which can be a powerful motivator for seeking change or forgiveness. 
Soul
• The soul is considered the essential part of a person, sometimes viewed as the source of one's moral and spiritual being.

Conscience
• The conscience is the internal faculty that allows a person to distinguish right from wrong.
• It functions as a moral guide or "compass" for the soul.
A healthy conscience can be a source of freedom, while a "seared" or ignored conscience can be dangerous, according to some interpretations. 
Guilt
• Guilt is the emotional and psychological response to having violated one's own conscience or sense of right and wrong.
• It is often described as a painful feeling or "bad feeling" that comes from knowing or thinking you have done something wrong.
• The intensity of guilt can depend on the perceived severity of the wrong action, both in relation to others and to oneself.
• Overcoming guilt often involves a process of seeking forgiveness, repenting, and trying to live according to one's conscience in the future. 

The statement "You have no conscience" describes a profound lack of morality and empathy. 
A conscience is the internal sense of right and wrong, and its absence means someone has no regard for the rights or feelings of others. Individuals without a conscience may be very antisocial, can be manipulative, and may not feel guilt or remorse for the harm they cause.

“NO WARRANT OF ARREST” vs. SEN. BATO DELA ROSA
On Nov 8, 2025 after Ombudsman Remulla’s pronouncement, the ICC (International Criminal Court) 
contradicts issuance of “Arrest Warrant” against Filipino Senator “Bato” Dela Rosa.

The official ICC site listing for the Philippines case mentions only the warrant for former President Duterte.

Bakit gustong-gusto nila sa Senado? Simple lang — para makapasok yung mga naka-barong at naka-kurbata na kurap. Doon, pwede nilang lapitan si Bryce, sabay bulong ng mga congressman-style na pananakot: “Pssst, Bryce… sumunod ka na, may lechon tayo sa lounge.” Kaya ayaw ni Bryce doon, kasi alam niyang ma-bra-brainwash siya.

Naalala n’yo pa noong panahon ni Duterte sa Bureau of Customs? Ganoon din ang style!

Kaya tama si Tito Sotto — Pasay City Jail ang tamang destinasyon! Doon, walang naka-kurbata na maglalakas-loob pumasok kasi madumi, mainit, at may kamera pa. Imagine si Jinggoy na papasok sa Pasay Jail naka-barong? Aba, baka siya pa ang interbyuhin ng mga preso: “Boss, may libreng load ka ba diyan?”

Kaya para fair, Pasay City Jail talaga ang the best. Walang VIP treatment, walang brainwashing — doon makikita kung sino ang tunay na matapang!

-  Juan Dela Cruz

column4:
Lumulubog ang ilang lugar sa Pilipinas dahil sa kombinasyon ng natural at gawa ng tao na mga dahilan. Narito ang ilan sa mga pangunahing sanhi:

1. Pagtaas ng Sea Level (Climate Change)

Dahil sa global warming, natutunaw ang mga yelo sa Arctic at Antarctica, na nagdudulot ng pagtaas ng lebel ng dagat. Ang mga baybaying lungsod tulad ng Manila, Malabon, Navotas, at Hagonoy ay unti-unting nalulubog.

2. Land Subsidence (Paglubog ng Lupa)

Ang sobrang pagkuha ng groundwater o deep well extraction ay nagdudulot ng pagbaba ng lupa.

Ang pagmimina at quarrying ay maaari ring magdulot ng pagguho at paglabas ng lupa, na nagiging sanhi ng unti-unting paglubog ng ilang lugar.

3. Pagtambak at Reclamation Projects

Ang mga reclamation projects ay nagbabago sa natural na daloy ng tubig, na nagiging sanhi ng pagbaha at paglubog ng mga kalapit na lugar.

4. Pagsira ng Mga Bakawan at Wetlands

Ang mga bakawan ay natural na depensa laban sa pagtaas ng tubig-dagat. Kapag nasira o tinayuan ng imprastraktura ang mga ito, mas bumibilis ang paglubog ng lupa.

5. Matinding Pagbaha at Bagyo

Dahil sa climate change, nagiging mas madalas at mas malalakas ang bagyo, na nagdudulot ng pagbaha at pagkatunaw ng lupa.

6. Likas na Paggalaw ng Lupa (Tectonic Activity)

Ang Pilipinas ay nasa Pacific Ring of Fire, kaya ang mga lindol at paggalaw ng fault lines ay maaaring magdulot ng pagbaba ng ilang bahagi ng lupa.

Mga Apektadong Lugar sa Pilipinas

Metro Manila (Malabon, Navotas, Manila, Pasay)

Bulacan (Hagonoy, Calumpit)

Pampanga (Masantol, Macabebe)

Zamboanga City

Iloilo City

Cebu City

Ano ang Pwedeng Gawin?

Bawasan ang paggamit ng deep wells at magpatupad ng maayos na water management.

Palakasin ang flood control systems tulad ng pumping stations at drainage systems.

Pangalagaan ang mga bakawan at wetlands bilang natural na depensa laban sa baha.

Limitahan ang mga reclamation projects na maaaring magdulot ng paglubog ng lupa.

Ang paglubog ng ilang lugar sa Pilipinas ay isang seryosong problema na nangangailangan ng pangmatagalang solusyon mula sa gobyerno, mga eksperto, at mamamayan.

One of the biggest problems we face today isn’t just corruption or misinformation — it’s how information is shared.
When people are interviewed or speak on issues, they often give explanations instead of showing the facts or teaching others how to verify them. That’s where confusion and bias begin.

Real understanding doesn’t come from opinions; it comes from access.
If the public could easily see the original documents — the contracts, the audit trails, the numbers — they wouldn’t have to depend on what anyone “explains.” They could decide for themselves.

What our nation needs isn’t more arguments; it’s education in truth.
Teach people how to investigate, how to read the data, how to check government sources.
Because when people can see the truth for themselves, they stop following sides — and start following facts.

Alam n’yo ba kung bakit todo pilit si Marcoleta na sa Senado ikulong si Bryce? Eh kasi aircon doon! Para bang VIP room ng kulungan — libre pa kape at WiFi siguro. Pero teka, Senado ba talaga kulungan? Syempre hindi! Ang tunay na kulungan ay Pasay City Jail.

Bakit gustong-gusto nila sa Senado? Simple lang — para makapasok yung mga naka-barong at naka-kurbata na kurap. Doon, pwede nilang lapitan si Bryce, sabay bulong ng mga congressman-style na pananakot: “Pssst, Bryce… sumunod ka na, may lechon tayo sa lounge.” Kaya ayaw ni Bryce doon, kasi alam niyang ma-bra-brainwash siya.

Naalala n’yo pa noong panahon ni Duterte sa Bureau of Customs? Ganoon din ang style!

Kaya tama si Tito Sotto — Pasay City Jail ang tamang destinasyon! Doon, walang naka-kurbata na maglalakas-loob pumasok kasi madumi, mainit, at may kamera pa. Imagine si Jinggoy na papasok sa Pasay Jail naka-barong? Aba, baka siya pa ang interbyuhin ng mga preso: “Boss, may libreng load ka ba diyan?”

Kaya para fair, Pasay City Jail talaga ang the best. Walang VIP treatment, walang brainwashing — doon makikita kung sino ang tunay na matapang!

-  Juan Dela Cruz

column4:
Chronology of events

1. Kumanta ang mga Discaya

2. (Same day) Pinalitan ang nga sumusunod:

Senate President
(From) ESCUDERO to SOTTO

Blue Ribbon Committee Char
(From) MARCOLETA to LACSON

3. (Today) Rinesbakan ni DOJ Secretary Remulla si ALCANTARA

4. (Today) Naglapag ng mga pangalan si ALCANTARA kabilang ang ilang mga senador.

Pero…

Hindi kasama si ROMUALDEZ sa mga pinangalanan.

5. (Today) DOJ sec Remulla requested the committee para maisama nya si ALCANTARA sa DOJ.

And was approved by the committee.

Comments:

1. Sa pagpapalit pa lang ng mga positions (see no 2), hindi ba obvious na na-alarma sila at kinailangan nilang kumilos to stop MARCOLETA?

2. Hindi rin ba obvious, that the core of the MISSION is to save ROMUALDEZ?

3. Hindi rin ba obvious, na nagpangalan nalang sila ng mga SENATORS para lang may maituro?

And to easily convince the public, syempre yung mga senador na dati ng nakulong ang pinili nila like Revilla, Estrada?

4. BIG QUEATION:
Where are Zaldy Co and Romualdez?

They are the biggest names in this issue. Their names came up many times in the hearings.
But where are they? Why haven’t they been called?

5.  The National Government (thru President) can easily do this OPERATION if they really wanted to.

Pero, di man lang sila nagpakita, kahit anino lang sana ng dalawang taong ito.

SEE…
This is not about who you support—Marcos, Leni, or Duterte.

This is about you…
You must carefully watch and observe what Congress and the Senate are doing—because this is about your stolen rights and your stolen money.

Don’t say, “we don’t know.”

Because it’s our responsibility as citizens to know and at least have a basic understanding of our government and our rights—so we can understand what’s really happening.

All of us pay taxes—on every product, there’s a tax; for regular employees, a portion is deducted from our salary every month.

I read this in a comment, and it made things clearer for me. It’s not about pink, yellow, or green—it’s simply about having a clean government for the next generation, because that is our right. 😌

column4:
Bago kayo mag comment dyan, dito tayo sa technicalities BASED sa Ph Constitution. Based on FACTS. PER CHAT GPT

Ano ang isyu?

Sen. Marcoleta at Sec. Remulla nagtalo tungkol sa Witness Protection Program (WPP).

May testigo (ex-DPWH official) na gustong pumasok sa WPP para magsalita tungkol sa anomalya sa flood control projects.

Sabi ni Remulla: Kahit hindi nakasulat sa batas, tinitingnan ng DOJ kung handang magbalik ng “ill-gotten money” (restitution) ang testigo para makita kung siya ay tapat at nasa good faith.

Sabi ni Marcoleta: Hindi tama na gawing requirement ang restitution, kasi wala ito sa batas. Ang WPP ay para protektahan ang testigo kapalit ng kanyang testimony, hindi kapalit ng pagbabalik ng pera.

Paano naging tama si Marcoleta?

Ayon sa RA 6981 (Witness Protection, Security and Benefit Act), ang mga kondisyon para mapasok sa WPP ay:

May mahalaga siyang testimony.

Nanganganib ang buhay o seguridad niya dahil sa testimony na iyon.

Hindi siya guilty ng mabigat na krimen na may moral turpitude.

Pumapayag siyang mag-testify.

👉 Walang binanggit ang batas tungkol sa restitution.

Kaya:

Legal side: Tama si Marcoleta — hindi puwedeng gawing requirement ang restitution kasi hindi ito nakasaad sa batas.

Practical side: May punto rin si Remulla — nakakatulong ang restitution para sa gobyerno at nagpapakita ng sincerity ng testigo, pero hindi ito dapat gawing kondisyon.
